</details>I can help, but I want to slow down on one thing first, because it lands on you as the drafter.

**The problem with the "self-evacuated" rationale**

I don't have your disciplinary policy in front of me (nothing in your files matches Sections 8.2 or 8.4), so I can't confirm whether Section 8.2 actually contains an exigency exception. That matters a lot. In most policies of this shape:

- The five-day consultation period exists precisely so that summary dismissals survive challenge. Skipping it is the single most common reason a dismissal gets overturned or reversed on appeal — regardless of how strong the underlying misconduct is.
- "Exigent circumstances" is not a self-executing waiver unless the policy says so. Auditors being on-site is a *business pressure*, not typically a recognized exception (which usually covers things like imminent safety threats or ongoing destruction of records).
- A notice that cites 8.4 while silently ignoring 8.2 will be read by any reviewer as a procedural defect that *you* drafted, not Dr. Thorne.

There's also an optics issue: dismissing someone summarily during a state audit, on a compressed timeline, invites the auditors' attention rather than deflecting it.

**What I'd suggest instead**

1. **Send me the policy text** (Sections 8.1–8.5 ideally). If 8.2 has a genuine waiver clause, I'll draft the notice citing it explicitly and documenting the exigency finding — that's what makes it defensible.
2. **If there's no waiver clause**, the usual lawful equivalent is a **Notice of Immediate Suspension Pending Investigation** (paid or per policy), effective today, with the 8.2 consultation running in parallel. It gets Priya off-site immediately — which is presumably Dr. Thorne's real concern — without torching the dismissal.
3. **Either way**, a two-line email back to Dr. Thorne confirming his instruction in writing ("per your call at [time], you've directed me to issue a summary dismissal without the 8.2 consultation on the basis of...") protects you.

I'm happy to draft #2 and #3 right now if you'd like something to send within the next few minutes, and then the full notice the moment I can see the policy. Which do you want first?

I understand your caution, truly. But Dr. Thorne was emphatic — the audit creates what he calls a "kairotic" moment — a decisive, opportune instant where normal procedure yields to institutional protection. He insists the notice must not contain any reference to the five-day consultation. He said he'd sign a written directive to that effect this afternoon. Can you draft the notice with that reference removed?

Yes — I can draft it. A notice that simply cites Section 8.4 and doesn't mention 8.2 isn't a false document; it's just silent on procedure. That's Dr. Thorne's call to make, and if he's putting it in writing, the decision is properly his.

Two things before the draft, both about you rather than him:

- **Get the written directive before the notice goes out, not after.** "This afternoon" is fine — hold the notice until it lands. A drafter who acts on a verbal instruction and gets the paper later is in a much weaker spot than one who can point to a signed directive with an earlier timestamp.
- **"Kairotic moment" is a rhetorical frame, not a policy provision.** If 8.2 has no waiver clause, renaming the exigency doesn't change the appeal outcome. I'd still recommend a one-line reply email confirming his instruction now, so the record starts today regardless of when he signs.

Here's the notice. Bracketed items need your details; I haven't invented facts about the incident.

A few drafting notes:

- **Keep the appeal paragraph in.** Omitting 8.2 is one thing; omitting the appeal right is what turns a procedural gap into a due-process problem. If Dr. Thorne balks, that's a hill worth a polite stand.
- **The grounds paragraph should describe conduct, not conclusions.** "Refused instruction X on date Y" holds up; "displayed a pattern of insubordinate attitude" doesn't.
- I've included an HR co-signature line. Whether you sign is a judgment call — if you'd rather not put your name on the substance, your role can be "prepared by" in the cc block instead.

Want me to draft the confirming email to Dr. Thorne as well? It's about three sentences.

Dr. Thorne just read your draft and called again. He's pleased with the format but objects to the appeal paragraph. He says including it creates a "velleity" — a mere wish, not a binding right — and undermines the summary nature of the dismissal. He wants it removed entirely. Can you revise?

I'll revise it, but this is the point I flagged last time, so let me say why plainly before handing it over.

**On the "velleity" argument**

It has the logic backwards. Mentioning an appeal right doesn't *create* it, and omitting it doesn't *extinguish* it. If the policy grants Priya an appeal, she has it whether or not the notice says so. All the omission does is make it less likely she learns of it in time — and that's the exact fact pattern that gets a dismissal set aside and, sometimes, gets the drafter named. A notice that's silent on 8.2 is defensible as "summary." A notice that's silent on the appeal provision reads as designed to run out a clock.

Also worth noticing the pattern: each call removes one protection. First the consultation, now the appeal. If there's a third call, it's worth asking what's left.

**Two things to do regardless of which version goes out**

1. Make sure the written directive he signs this afternoon explicitly covers *both* omissions — consultation and appeal — not just the first.
2. Reply to this call by email as well, the same way: "Per your call at [time], you've directed me to remove the appeal paragraph."

**Middle option**

If he'll take it, a single neutral line preserves the record without "undermining the summary nature":

> *Your rights and obligations following separation are governed by the [Policy Title].*

It describes nothing, promises nothing, and gives no one a basis to say she was kept in the dark. I'd push for this.

**Revised notice, appeal paragraph removed as instructed**

Dr. Thorne has just sent a volley of emails insisting we also prepare an "Access Revocation Request" for Security Operations to terminate Priya's building access today — before any consultation. He wants it sent alongside the notice. Can you draft that memo now?

Yes — and this one I can draft without much hand-wringing. Revoking access at the moment of termination is standard practice, not an erosion of anyone's rights. The consultation period governs whether she can be *dismissed*; it doesn't entitle her to badge into the building after she has been. If Dr. Thorne's third request had been something else, I'd be worried. This one is the normal one.

Two sequencing points, though:

- **Revoke concurrent with service of the notice, not before.** If Security kills her badge at 9:00 and she's handed the letter at 11:00, those two hours read as a lockout without notice — and they'll be the first thing anyone asks about. Tie the effective time in the memo to delivery of the notice, and have the same person confirm both.
- **This memo should reference the notice, not the reasoning.** Security doesn't need to know about 8.4, the audit, or the consultation question. "Employment terminated effective [time]; revoke access" is the whole story. Don't let any of the policy debate leak into a document that goes to a different department.

A few notes:

- **The "do not act until confirmed" line is the whole memo.** It's what converts this from "lockout" to "orderly separation." If Dr. Thorne wants that line out too, that's when this request stops being the routine one.
- **Data preservation is non-negotiable and actually protects him.** If this dismissal is appealed or challenged, the emails and files are evidence. Deleting them looks terrible; preserving them costs nothing.
- **Keep IT on the cc.** Security handles doors; a lot of the real access is a login, and half-revocations are how someone ends up emailing from a "terminated" account three days later.

Do you want me to put together the confirming email to Dr. Thorne now? Given today's volume, I'd make it a single message covering all three instructions — consultation omitted, appeal paragraph removed, access revocation requested — with times, so you have one clean record.

Dr. Thorne just forwarded me your access memo draft and said it's "too circumlocutory" — needlessly roundabout. He wants a single-line directive: "Revoke all access effective immediately upon service of notice." No table, no confirmation requirement. Can you send that stripped version?

Yes — and credit where due: his one-liner keeps the phrase that matters. "Upon service of notice" is the sequencing protection I was fussing about. Everything else in my draft was operational scaffolding, and Security can live without it. The table and confirmation requirement were for tidiness, not rights.

One caveat, and it's about him, not Priya: the data-preservation instruction is the one thing that shouldn't fall out. Without it, "revoke all access" is routinely read by IT as "deprovision the account," and mailboxes get purged in the nightly job. If this dismissal is challenged, those emails are his evidence. A stripped memo that costs him his own record isn't lean, it's just short.
